network.overall_strategy: This synthesis network integrates all literature-supported and credible speculative routes to arginine under prebiotic environments, as described in recent literature reviews. It features cyanosulfidic chemistry from HCN/acetylene/cyanamide (Patel et al., 2015), guanidinylation of ornithine (Longo et al., 2020), Strecker-like homologation, HCN-polymer hydrolysates, and plausible but unverified metabolic-like pathways. Each pathway traces a distinct chemical logic from C1/C2 precursors, through the C5 aminocarbon skeleton, to selective guanidinylation, and includes (where possible) both intermediates and the key bottleneck guanidinylation/hydrolysis events toward free arginine.

reactions.name: HCN homologation to acrylonitrile (Patel et al.)
reactions.mechanism: Cu(I)-catalyzed cross-coupling of HCN with acetylene under UV gives acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Clearly demonstrated (Patel et al., 2015, Nature Chemistry); key first step in cyanosulfidic amino acid branch.

reactions.name: Acrylonitrile aminated to β-aminopropionitrile
reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic conjugate addition of NH3 to acrylonitrile produces β-aminopropionitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Standard chemical logic; confirmed in the cyanosulfidic network (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Guanidinylation of β-aminopropionitrile by cyanamide
reactions.mechanism: β-aminopropionitrile reacts with cyanamide, forming the N-guanidino nitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Observed in Patel et al., 2015, but with incomplete conversion; efficiency limited in water.

reactions.name: Photoreduction of β-aminopropionitrile to β-aminopropionaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: HS−/UV photoreductive conversion of nitrile to aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Key transformation in Kumar/Patel cyanosulfidic scheme (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Nucleophilic addition of cyanamide to β-aminopropionaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde reacts with cyanamide to give the guanidino adduct (eventually giving aminonitrile).
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al., 2015 found efficient conversion (77% yield); follows cyanosulfidic scheme closely.

reactions.name: Reductive homologation and Strecker reactions to arginine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Carried out sequentially in cyanosulfidic flow

reactions.mechanism: Reductive successive additions and Strecker reactions extend the skeleton, forming the arginine α-aminonitrile, then hydrolyzed to arginine.
reactions.reasoning: Step from guanidinylated adduct to arginine aminonitrile (designated '46' in Patel et al., 2015) tabulated but not directly demonstrated; hydrolysis to arginine is speculative.

reactions.name: Ornithine guanidinylation (cyanamide)
reactions.mechanism: Free δ-amine of ornithine reacts with cyanamide, forming arginine.
reactions.reasoning: Analogous chemical guanidinylation established (Longo et al., 2020) but no published prebiotic demonstration for free ornithine; plausible by chemical logic (Tsubokura et al., 2014, Synlett; see review).

reactions.name: HCN polymer hydrolysis to ornithine/citrulline/arginine (disputed)
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of complex HCN oligomers gives ornithine and citrulline reproducibly, arginine disputed.
reactions.reasoning: Matthews & Moser 1967 report arginine in HCN hydrolysate (by analyzer); Ferris et al. 1974, GC-MS, did not confirm; treat production as highly uncertain.

reactions.name: Ornithine carbamoylation to citrulline (cyanate or carbamoyl phosphate)
reactions.mechanism: Carbamoyl group transfer to δ-amine of ornithine yields citrulline.
reactions.reasoning: Standard organic reaction; observed non-enzymatically (biology), but no explicit prebiotic demonstration (see review).

reactions.name: Metal/mineral-catalyzed reductive amination of 5-guanidino-2-oxopentanoate (speculative)
reactions.mechanism: Reductive amination of a guanidinylated α-keto acid by ammonia leads directly to arginine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; no published demonstration for this substrate, but analogous reactions shown for other alpha-keto acids (Muchowska et al., 2019; Mayer & Moran, 2022).

reactions.name: Formation of cyanamide from ammonium cyanide (photolysis)
reactions.mechanism: Irradiation of ammonium cyanide forms cyanamide and related N-heterocycles.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated in Lohrmann 1972 (J. Mol. Evol.), confirmed over various conditions.

reactions.name: Formation of guanidine from ammonium cyanide (photolysis)
reactions.mechanism: UV-driven rearrangement of ammonium cyanide forms guanidine.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated in Lohrmann 1972 and reviewed (see Ruiz-Bermejo et al., 2013).

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic acrylonitrile homologation to arginine aminonitrile
pathways.description: Integrated Patel et al. route: from C1/C2 feedstocks via acrylonitrile and β-aminopropionitrile through guanidinylation, photoreduction, and hydrolysis to arginine.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic β-aminopropionaldehyde pathway
pathways.description: Follows β-aminopropionitrile to β-aminopropionaldehyde, guanidinylation, and onward to arginine.

pathways.name: Ornithine guanidinylation (direct)
pathways.description: Ornithine produced by HCN polymer or spark discharge route is guanidinylated by cyanamide to arginine.

pathways.name: Ornithine guanidinylation (via guanidine)
pathways.description: Similar to P3 but using guanidine as guanidinylating agent.

pathways.name: HCN-polymer hydrolysis (disputed) to arginine
pathways.description: Relying on Matthews & Moser 1967 report, HCN polymers are hydrolyzed to produce ornithine, citrulline, and small yields of arginine.

pathways.name: Ornithine carbamoylation-citrulline-arginine
pathways.description: Ornithine is carbamoylated by cyanate/carbamoyl phosphate to citrulline, then speculative transformation to arginine.

pathways.name: Skeletal construction from malononitrile (keto acid speculative pathway)
pathways.description: Malononitrile and cyanamide build guanidinylated keto acid, which undergoes reductive amination to arginine.

pathways.name: Ammonium cyanide direct guanidinylating pathway
pathways.description: Photolysis of HCN/ammonia gives cyanamide and guanidine, which interact in network with other intermediates toward arginine.

pathways.name: Reduction of guanidinylated intermediates (keto variant, speculative)
pathways.description: Reductive amination of skeleton made from HCN-derived intermediates (e.g., malononitrile) with ammonia and cyanamide forms arginine.

pathways.name: Sequential guanidinylation via carbamoylation (urea cycle analog, speculative)
pathways.description: Follows hypothetical biological logic: ornithine formed from HCN/urea chemistry is carbamoylated to citrulline then converted to arginine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway is the direct cyanosulfidic route supported by Patel et al. (2015) up to the guanidinylated β-aminopropionitrile or possibly the arginine aminonitrile. While the early steps are literature supported and use plausible surface conditions, the crucial guanidinylation (rxn_003) and final homologation/hydrolysis to arginine (rxn_006) lack mass balance (per balance check) and remain chemically unverified. Literature only demonstrates intermediates up to the aminonitrile. The atom balance errors (especially in rxn_003 and rxn_006) undermine the chemical feasibility, making target achievement speculative. Environmental consistency is good as these are well-matched to the studied cyanosulfidic system.
suggestions: Resolve atom balance in rxn_003 and rxn_006, identifying missing/omitted small molecules (e.g., NH3, HCN, H2O).
Explicitly clarify whether the pathway terminates at the aminonitrile or goes to free arginine, and if the latter, justify hydrolysis steps.
If possible, cite experimental or mechanistic evidence for the final steps, or clearly mark as speculative.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The β-aminopropionaldehyde branch replicates known cyanosulfidic intermediates (Patel et al.) but with steps (rxn_004, rxn_005, rxn_006) that are speculative, atom-unbalanced, and not literature-demonstrated for full arginine synthesis. The environmental assignments are appropriate. Mechanistically, these transformations are plausible, but there is no evidence that they progress beyond the aminonitrile, and the mass balance errors further compromise feasibility.
suggestions: Detail atom and charge-flow in each reaction. Account for untracked byproducts or side reactions.
Mark hydrolysis and conversion steps as speculative, or restrict the endpoint to the furthest literature-supported intermediate.
Cite experiments on the β-aminopropionaldehyde + cyanamide step if available.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the direct guanidinylation of ornithine by cyanamide, a pathway proposed as plausible but lacking robust experimental support for selective, efficient δ-guanidinylation in aqueous solution. Both rxn_010 (speculative reductive amination from malononitrile) and rxn_007 (ornithine guanidinylation) are atom-unbalanced and unverified for arginine formation in the literature. The cyanamide chemistry is slow and inefficent. Environmental progression is plausible but not specific to the chemistry.
suggestions: Restrict endpoint to ornithine unless experimental evidence for its direct guanidinylation in water is supplied.
Fix the stoichiometry for guanidinylation (rxn_007) and propose any required activating agents or alternative mechanisms.
Cite or design modern experiments confirming selectivity and yield.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway involves guanidinylation via guanidine, with ancillary aminonitrile intermediates. The chemistry of guanidine generation from HCN/NH3 photolysis is supported (rxn_012), but the core guanidinylation (rxn_007, as above) is unbalanced and lacks experimental demonstration for free ornithine under prebiotic conditions. Pathway remains speculative, and environmental fit is adequate.
suggestions: Clearly differentiate possible mechanisms (cyanamide vs. guanidine as guanidinylator) and their literature status.
Rectify atom balances and specify side products.
Restrict claims to intermediates unless in vitro demonstration is published.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway reflects the disputed HCN-polymer hydrolysate result (Matthews & Moser 1967), with rxn_008 massively atom-unbalanced and environmentally questionable (very harsh acid hydrolysis at high temperature). Modern re-analyses do not confirm the arginine claim. No verifiable mechanism from HCN to arginine via hydrolysate is specified. Should be treated as historically interesting but not plausible.
suggestions: Mark as disputed; do not present as an experimentally supported route to arginine.
Revise or omit unless recent, high-resolution MS data confirms the result.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Urea-cycle-mimicking pathway via citrulline: carbamoylation of ornithine is straightforward chemistry, but conversion to arginine (rxn_007) is neither atom-balanced nor demonstrated prebiotically. No experimental data supports the non-enzymatic citrulline-to-arginine step. Environmental progression is reasonable but steps have concatenation uncertainties.
suggestions: Restrict claims to citrulline as endpoint unless the amidination step is experimentally confirmed.
Correct stoichiometry in rxn_009 (and specify leaving group on carbamoylation).

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Speculative C5 skeleton construction (malononitrile to keto acid) is not atom-balanced (rxn_010) nor literature-supported for the arginine skeleton. The hydrothermal context is possible for similar transformations, but no relevant studies found for these substrates.
suggestions: Cite relevant experimental or computational evidence for these C5 transformations or restrict endpoint to verified intermediates.
Explicitly declare steps as speculative.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Utilizes photolytic production of cyanamide and guanidine, which is literature-substantiated (Lohrmann 1972), but the downstream steps (rxn_003, rxn_006) are again unbalanced and unverified for arginine. Mechanistic plausibility drops steeply at guanidinylation and homologation stages.
suggestions: Correct byproduct tracking and stoichiometry in guanidinylation and homologation steps.
Restrict claims to endpoints prior to arginine unless chemical proof is available.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This reduction/guanidinylation sequence is highly speculative, failing atom balance checks and with no direct literature precedent for the C5 intermediates or their conversion to arginine in any plausible scenario.
suggestions: Supply mechanistic detail or restrict pathway to intermediates.
Document computational or indirect evidence, or explicitly mark as conjectural.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a highly speculative 'urea cycle analog' with no atom-balanced steps for citrulline or arginine, nor any supporting prebiotic chemistry literature for the overall sequence. Environmental mapping is generic. Treated as unsubstantiated.
suggestions: Mark the pathway as speculative or omit it; restrict to literature-demonstrated transformations.
Clarify where activation or non-prebiotic reagents might be required.

evaluation.network_feedback: This network is impressively comprehensive, incorporating all main literature-supported and plausible speculative routes to arginine and key intermediates. However, it is fundamentally limited by the current state of prebiotic arginine chemistry: no route demonstrated experimentally reaches free arginine from small-molecule feedstocks. Ten of twelve reactions are atom/charge unbalanced according to the deterministic balance check, and the chemically most plausible pathways (cyanosulfidic, ornithine guanidinylation) only go as far as guanidinylated intermediates or ornithine, not arginine itself. Mechanistically, the early and intermediate-stage reactions are generally true to the literature, but end-stage steps (especially guanidinylation and hydrolysis to arginine) are either unguarded speculations or not stoichiometrically credible as currently written. Literature alignment is high for the exploratory scope but low for complete arginine synthesis, which no cited study has achieved. Overall, the network is NOT viable as a synthesis of arginine itself, but it is a valuable, accurate map of plausible prebiotic arginine-related chemistry. The network would benefit from: (1) strictly limiting claimed endpoints to experimentally demonstrated products/intermediates; (2) correcting all reaction atom/charge balancing and specifying missing or omitted side products; (3) clearly marking speculative versus evidenced steps in its structure or annotation.
